lessons.title: Reading Property Price Data Honestly: RBI HPI, NHB RESIDEX and Listing Prices

children.text: In the same week, you might see four claims about your city. A WhatsApp forward says prices jumped 15% this year. A property portal shows average asking prices up 18% in your locality. A consultant's report says average launch prices rose 10%. And your neighbour sold a ten-year-old flat for barely more than the purchase price. It is tempting to think three of these are lying. Usually none of them is. They are simply measuring different things. By the end of this lesson you will know what each kind of price number really measures, how to read the RBI and NHB indices, and the traps that make appreciation look bigger than it is.

body.text: Every property price number answers a narrower question than it appears to. Before you trust one, ask four things: whose price, which homes, as of when, and measured how.

children.text: Four Kinds of Price Numbers

body.caption: Where Indian property price numbers come from

cells: Asking prices of homes currently advertised
Up to date and available at locality level
Not transactions; stale and inflated listings; ignores negotiation
Consultant and research reports (such as Anarock, Knight Frank, JLL, PropEquity)
Mostly new-launch prices, sales and unsold inventory
Timely, detailed data on launches and absorption
Skewed towards new projects; methods differ between firms
Circle rates, ready reckoner rates, guidance values
Government minimum values for stamp duty
Revised irregularly; can sit well above or below market prices
Systematic city-level indices from registrations or loan valuations
Published with a lag; city averages hide micro-markets

children.text: The RBI House Price Index

markDefs.definition: A number that tracks how prices change relative to a base period, which is set to 100. An index of 150 means prices are 50% higher than in the base period.
The reference period against which an index is measured, where the index is set to exactly 100.

children.text: The Reserve Bank of India publishes a quarterly House Price Index built from property registration data supplied by state registration authorities. It covers ten major cities, including Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Chennai, Kolkata and Ahmedabad, and combines them into an all-India figure. Like every
price index
, it is measured against a
base period
set to 100, which for the RBI series is 2010-11. Because it uses registered transactions, it reflects prices people actually paid, not prices they hoped for.
NHB RESIDEX

The National Housing Bank publishes RESIDEX, a quarterly residential price index covering 50 cities, so it reaches well beyond the metros into cities like Coimbatore, Indore and Bhubaneswar. It reports two measures: prices based on property valuations carried out by banks and housing finance companies when they sanction home loans, and market prices for under-construction properties collected from developers. The current series uses 2017-18 as its base year.

columns.label: RBI House Price Index
points: Ten major cities plus an all-India figure
Best for long-run trends in large metros

columns.label: NHB RESIDEX
points: Built from bank and HFC loan valuations, plus developer prices for under-construction homes
Best for comparing ready and under-construction trends across more cities

body.label: RBI DBIE: Database on Indian Economy
body.description: RBI's statistics portal, where the House Price Index series and other housing data are published.

body.label: NHB RESIDEX
body.description: National Housing Bank's residential price index portal, with city-level index values.

children.text: Reading an Index Correctly
An index level on its own tells you almost nothing. What matters is the change between two dates. To compare periods of different lengths, turn that change into a compound annual growth rate.

body.caption: n = number of years between the two index readings.

body.title: Index to annual growth
body.prompt: A city's house price index stood at 180 six years ago and stands at 240 today. What is the compound annual growth rate of prices? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Total change = 240 ÷ 180 − 1 = 33.3%. CAGR = (240 ÷ 180)^(1/6) − 1 = 1.3333^(0.1667) − 1 = 4.91% a year. A headline of "prices up 33%" sounds far more exciting than under 5% a year, yet they describe exactly the same data.

body.title: Compare two cities
body.question: Using the same house price index series with the same base year, Mumbai's index is 250 and Kochi's is 300. Which statement is correct?
options: Homes in Kochi are more expensive than homes in Mumbai
Prices in Kochi have risen more than prices in Mumbai since the base year
Mumbai's prices have fallen since the base year
Kochi's index proves it is the better place to invest today
body.explanation: Each city's index starts at 100 in the base year, so the index shows growth, not price level. Kochi prices have tripled since the base year and Mumbai's have risen 2.5 times, but a Mumbai flat can still cost several times more than a Kochi flat. Past growth also says nothing certain about future returns.

children.text: The Mix Trap

markDefs.definition: When an average price changes because the type of homes being sold changes, not because the same homes became more or less valuable.

children.text: Many headlines report the average price per square foot of homes sold or launched. That average can rise sharply even when no home has become more valuable, simply because more expensive homes made up a bigger share of sales. This is the
mix effect
, and it matters a lot in Indian cities where developers have shifted launches towards luxury projects.

body.caption: A micro-market where no home changed price (illustrative, equal-sized units)

cells: Average price per sq ft of homes sold

body.title: How much did the average rise?
body.prompt: Using the table above, calculate the Year 2 average price per sq ft, then find how much the average rose from Year 1 to Year 2, in percent. Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Year 2 average = (500 × ₹8,000 + 500 × ₹20,000) ÷ 1,000 = ₹14,000. Rise = ₹14,000 ÷ ₹10,400 − 1 = 34.6%. A report could honestly say "average prices up 34.6%", yet every single home is worth exactly what it was a year ago. Only the mix of homes sold changed.

body.title: How good indices avoid the mix trap

children.text: Repeat-sales method:
tracks the same property each time it is sold, so the change reflects genuine appreciation of that home.
Hedonic method:
adjusts prices for features such as size, age, floor and location, estimating what a standard home would sell for in each period.
Weighting and stratification:
breaks the market into segments or localities and weights them consistently over time, so a surge in luxury sales does not distort the whole figure.
When a report quotes a simple average price per square foot without explaining its method, assume the mix effect may be at work.
One Flat, Four Prices

markDefs.definition: The minimum value a state government sets for a property for stamp duty. Called circle rate in Delhi, ready reckoner rate in Maharashtra and guidance value in Karnataka.

children.text: Take a single two-bedroom flat in Andheri East, Mumbai. On the same day, it can carry four very different values. None of them is the flat's "true" appreciation until you know which one you are looking at. The lowest is often the
ready reckoner rate
value, which the state uses to calculate stamp duty.

stats.label: Bank valuation
stats.context: What the lender assessed for the loan

children.text: The listing is 8% above the price the buyer actually paid. If you had bought this flat for ₹1 crore and judged your appreciation from the portal, you would think you had made 35%. The registered transaction says 25%. The difference is not a rounding error. It is the gap between hope and reality.

body.text: Ready reckoner and circle rates are not market prices, but they matter at tax time. If you sell a property for less than its stamp duty value, income tax rules can treat the stamp duty value as your sale price when calculating capital gains, subject to a small tolerance. Check the current rules with a chartered accountant before agreeing to a price below the government rate.

body.title: Name the government rate
body.textWithBlank: In Maharashtra, the government's minimum property values used to calculate stamp duty are called ___ rates.
body.explanation: Maharashtra publishes ready reckoner rates. Delhi calls them circle rates, and Karnataka calls them guidance values. All three set a floor for stamp duty, not a market price.

body.title: The family success story
body.scenario: At a family wedding in Lucknow, Deepa's uncle announces: "I bought my flat in 1995 for ₹5 lakh. Today a broker says it is worth ₹2 crore. Property never fails. Forget mutual funds and buy land." Deepa, who has been investing through SIPs on Zerodha, wants to respond sensibly.
body.prompt: Calculate the annual growth rate implied by the story. Then list the problems with using this story as evidence that property always beats other investments.
body.modelAnswer:
1. ₹5 lakh to ₹2 crore over 30 years is a 40-fold rise. CAGR = 40^(1/30) − 1 = about 13.1% a year. Impressive, but not magical over three decades.
2. "A broker says" is not a transaction. The ₹2 crore is an estimate, possibly a listing-style number. A real sale might close lower, and selling brokerage would come off the top.
3. It ignores costs: stamp duty and registration at purchase, 30 years of maintenance, property tax and repairs, none of which are in the 13.1%.
4. It ignores inflation. Much of any 30-year rise is simply rupees losing value. The next lesson shows how to strip it out.
5. It is one success story. Nobody at the wedding describes the flat in a stalled project, the plot with a title dispute, or the area that never developed. This is survivorship bias.
6. It compares an investment with a known outcome to a vague idea of other options. A fair comparison would check what ₹5 lakh in a broad Indian equity index fund or a mix of assets would have become over the same years, after costs.
7. A sensible response: the uncle's flat did well, but the right question is not whether property can work. It is whether a specific property at today's price, with today's yields, is likely to beat the alternatives.

body.title: Before you trust a price growth claim
steps: Identify the source: listing, consultant report, government rate or official index.
Check whether it measures asking prices, new-launch prices or registered transactions.
Ask which homes are included: the whole city, one micro-market, new launches only or all sales.
Look for the mix effect: is the average rising because more luxury homes are being sold?
Convert any total change into a CAGR using the exact number of years.
Check the date: official indices are published with a lag.
Compare with RBI HPI or NHB RESIDEX for the same city and period.

cards.definition: RBI's quarterly index from registered transactions in ten major cities, with 2010-11 as base.
National Housing Bank's quarterly index covering 50 cities, using loan valuations and developer prices, with 2017-18 as base.
The reference period in which an index is set to 100.
A change in average price caused by a change in the type of homes sold, not by appreciation.
Maharashtra's government minimum property value for stamp duty; circle rate in Delhi, guidance value in Karnataka.
An index built by tracking price changes of the same properties across repeated sales.
Drawing conclusions only from success stories while ignoring investments that failed.

points: Listing prices, consultant reports, government rates and official indices each measure something different, so they rarely agree.
RBI's House Price Index uses registered transactions in ten major cities; NHB RESIDEX uses loan valuations and developer prices across 50 cities.
An index level shows growth since its base year, not how expensive a city is.
Convert total changes into CAGR: a 33% rise over six years is under 5% a year.
Average price per square foot can rise sharply with no real appreciation because of the mix effect.
Judge your own appreciation from registered transaction prices, not portal listings or brokers' estimates.
Family success stories suffer from survivorship bias and usually ignore costs and inflation.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or tax advice. The people, properties, index values and prices shown are illustrative. Index methods, coverage and base years can be revised, and tax rules on property sales change, so check the latest publications from RBI and NHB and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser or a chartered accountant before making any decision.
